ABSTRACT 44

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies demonstrate potent anti-tumor efficacy in hematologic 45

malignancies, yet clinical outcomes remain unpredictable due to the bespoke nature of the treatment, 46

which is manufactured from each patient’s own T-cells. While germline variants are known to influence 47

response to immune checkpoint inhibitors1,2, their role in CAR-T cell therapy is unknown. Here, we pair 48

whole-genome germline sequencing of lymphoma patients from the ZUMA-13 and ZUMA-74 clinical 49

trials of axicabtagene ciloleucel, along with correlative biomarkers and functional assays, to ascertain the 50

impact of germline variants on CAR-T cell behavior.  Hypothesizing shared mechanisms of the most 51

common toxicities of CAR-T cells, namely cytokine release syndrome (CRS) with hemophagocytic 52

lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)—a hyperinflammatory syndrome driven by T cell overactivation5, we first 53

looked within 17 canonical HLH-associated genes6, and identified putative deleterious STXBP2 variants 54

in 15% of ZUMA-1 patients with toxicity, which were absent in control subjects who did not experience 55

high grade toxicity. Subjects with these variants had elevated baseline IFN-γ and inflammatory cytokines, 56

findings that were recapitulated in engineered STXBP2-deficient and STXBP2-variant-expressing primary 57

CAR-T cells derived from healthy donors. However, STXBP2 variant enrichment was absent in ZUMA-7 58

for this toxicity phenotype, possibly reflecting differences in underlying disease burden and evolving 59

clinical management between the trials. A more expansive genome-wide analysis revealed ADAMTSL3 (a 60

negative regulator of TGFβ7) as the only gene nominally enriched for putative deleterious variants in both 61

ZUMA-1 and ZUMA-7 among control subjects, suggesting a protective effect. Finally, we focused on 62

associations between germline variants and CAR-T cell expansion after infusion, a more objective and 63

granular continuous variable that is strongly associated with clinical response across most CAR-T 64

products8. We found a strong association between PTPN22, a known negative regulator of T-cell 65

activation 9–12 and an autoimmune risk gene13,14, variant status and CAR-T cell expansion in both ZUMA- 66

1 and ZUMA-7, with the patients having the highest level of CAR-T expansion across clinical trials 67

harboring variants in the gene. Together, these findings demonstrate the first clear association between 68

INTRODUCTION 72

Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has changed the clinical landscape of hematologic 73

malignancies, with an ever-growing number of FDA approvals since 20173,15–20. Clinical use of CAR T 74

cell products has generally been limited to tertiary academic centers due to the need for close monitoring 75

for two class-effect cytokine-related toxicities, namely cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune 76

effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), either of which can be fatal21. Unlike 77

traditional therapeutics that are essentially identical across all patients, CAR-T cells are bespoke and 78

harbor all of the ancestral genetic polymorphisms of their parental T-cells. Attempts to predict CAR-T 79

cell behavior have been limited to the use of existing tumor burden or traditional lab parameters, but fail 80

to account for the complexities of these living drugs22,23. In the context of another immunotherapy, 81

immune checkpoint blockade therapy, a detailed survey of immune-related inherited polymorphisms 82

revealed that the gain of a cryptic exon for IL-7, a critical regulator of lymphocyte homeostasis, is 83

strongly associated with immune-related adverse events1, demonstrating the importance of the host 84

genetic state in the clinical behavior of immunotherapy. 85

86

The biochemical and clinical phenotype of CRS is similar to the rare hyperinflammatory syndrome 87

hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Both share a putative mechanism in which highly activated 88

T cells produce cytokines (like IFN-γ) that spur myeloid production of inflammatory mediators (like IL-6, 89

IL-1, and TNFα), which drive systemic toxicities5,24. Among the known etiologies driving HLH are loss- 90

of-function (LOF) germline variants in cytolytic pathways, which display variable penetrance and 91

phenotypic effects6,25–27. While initial HLH studies identified only biallelic loss-of-function variants as 92

causative of classical, familial HLH, which typically presents in childhood, a more nuanced 93

understanding now includes heterozygous LOF variants in granule-dependent cytotoxicity gene members, 94

which can result in HLH in the context of significant immunologic challenge26,28–33 and/or later in 95

adulthood. 96

We initially hypothesized that germline variants in HLH-associated genes could modulate CAR-T cell 98

behavior and immune response, resulting in clinically meaningful phenomena. To maximize the ability to 99

explore the full range of variants potentially relevant in this clinical setting, we performed whole genome 100

germline sequencing and correlative analyses with biomarkers and functional assays to study variants in 101

two clinical trials of axicabtagene ciloleucel in patients with aggressive lymphoma, the ZUMA-13 (n=86 102

evaluable subjects) and ZUMA-7 (n=150 evaluable subjects) clinical trials4. We find genomic, correlative 103

cytokine, and corroborative bioassay evidence linking specific germline genomic variants to CAR-T cell 104

behavior in the clinical and experimental settings. 105

RESULTS 107

Study Participants 108

A total of 86 patients with aggressive lymphomas who received axicabtagene ciloleucel as part of 109

ZUMA-13 underwent whole genome sequencing (Extended Data Fig. 1-3). Of those patients, 41 reached 110

the combined toxicity endpoint (either high-grade CRS, Neurotoxicity-Events (NE, now known as 111

immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome ICANS), or those who received tocilizumab; 112

further details in methods) and were included in the toxicity cohort, while 43 patients had no or reduced 113

toxicity and were considered the control cohort. Two patients from the toxicity cohort and four from the 114

control cohorts were excluded during quality control steps (Methods), leaving 39 patients in each cohort. 115

Consistent with prior studies, inflammatory cytokines related to CAR-T cell toxicity (GM-CSF, IFN-γ, 116

MCP-1, and TNFα) were similar between the two cohorts at baseline; however, peak levels after infusion 117

were significantly elevated in the toxicity cohort, though for some cytokines, the absolute magnitude of 118

the difference was small (Table 1). Peak IL-6, which is a known driver of cytokine storm24 , was 119

significantly higher in the toxicity cohort than the control cohort; however, receipt of IL-6 blockade for 120

CAR-T cell toxicity confounds measurement of this cytokine 3,5,34,35. Baseline characteristics, including 121

age, sex, and tumor response rates at 1 month, were similar between the cohorts. 122

Clinical and biochemical profiles of patients with STXBP2 putative deleterious variants 211

To explore the clinical profile of patients with putative deleterious variants in STXBP2, we analyzed the 212

time at which patients developed significant toxicity (as defined by the combined toxicity endpoint). By 213

day 10 after CAR-T infusion, all patients with STXBP2 putative deleterious variants reached the 214

combined toxicity endpoint (though with similar rates of high-grade neurologic toxicity 67% vs 72%, and 215

CRS 17% vs 13% to the broader study), while only half of the remaining total patients met any of the 216

toxicity endpoints (100% vs. 50%, p=0.0015) (Fig. 1d). Moreover, STXBP2 putative deleterious variant 217

carriers reached the combined toxicity endpoint more quickly, at a median of 5 days after CAR-T infusion 218

compared to 7 days for those non-carriers who reached the combined toxicity endpoint. Furthermore, 219

when patients whose sole criterion of the toxicity endpoint was receipt of tocilizumab were removed, we 220

found a trend towards earlier development of high-grade CRS or neurologic toxicity among STXBP2 221

variant carriers (p=0.1, Extended Data Fig. 13). This was true for both the CRS and neurotoxicity 222

components of the combined toxicity endpoint, with median day of high-grade CRS onset (4 vs. 6.5 days) 223

and neurotoxicity (6 vs. 7 days) for variant carriers versus the remaining toxicity cohort, respectively. 224

Consequences of STXBP2 loss in CAR-T cells 262

We then sought to model the effects of STXBP2 deficiency in CAR-T cells engineered from healthy 263

donors. We generated αCD19-CD28 CAR-T cells (similar in design to the axicabtagene ciloleucel 264

transgene), in which CRISPR-Cas9 was utilized to knock out STXBP2 (Fig. 2b and 2c) in primary 265

healthy donor T cells. In an experiment modeled on the NK-degranulation assay used for clinical 266

diagnosis of HLH53, we co-cultured the CAR-T cells with CD19-expressing K562 stimulator cells and 267

assessed short-term degranulation by measuring levels of lysosome-associated membrane protein-1 268

(LAMP-1/ CD107a), which represents turnover of the interior cytotoxic granules in lymphocytes. 269

STXBP2-KO CAR T cells demonstrated significantly impaired degranulation, impaired cytotoxicity 270

(CD8+=p=.0023, CD4+ p=<.0001), and increased intracellular IFN-γ production (CD4+ p=.0028, but not 271

strictly statistically significant for CD8+ cells p=.058, Fig. 2d-i, Extended Data Fig. 17). 272

DISCUSSION 342

CAR-T cell therapy is a critical tool for the treatment of advanced hematologic malignancies, but 343

inherited genetic drivers of their activity are still largely unexplored, representing an unmet need to better 344

understand the underlying biological processes. In this study, we leveraged an integrative computational 345

and functional approach to identify enrichment of putative deleterious variants among patients who had 346

aggressive large cell lymphoma patients and had received axicabtagene ciloleucel in the ZUMA-1 and 347

ZUMA-7 trials. Interrogating the complex phenotype of CAR-T cell-related toxicity and limiting our 348

search to HLH-associated genes, we found enrichment of subjects with putative deleterious variants in 349

STXBP2 in ZUMA-1, and in vitro studies leveraging CRISPR-Cas9 to generate near-complete loss of 350

function mutations, or the overexpression of variant STXBP2 proteins, were consistent with reduced 351

degranulation and increased cytokine production. However, we did not find enrichment of STXBP2 352

variants in subjects enrolled in the ZUMA-7 trial who experienced toxicity. 353

Broadening our search to the entire genome but this time including germline sequencing data from both 355

clinical trials of axicabtagene ciloleucel, the most nominally significant finding across both cohorts with 356

respect to toxicity was the enrichment of ADAMTSL3 putative deleterious variants among control cohort 357

subjects (i.e., those who did not experience severe toxicity), suggesting a possible protective effect from 358

CAR-T associated toxicities. Finally, we found strong cross-cohort enrichment of PTPN22 putative 359

deleterious variant carriers among subjects with the highest levels of CAR-T expansion. 360

361

STXBP2 plays a critical role in cytotoxic granule membrane fusion in lymphocyte granule-mediated 362

cytotoxicity. Recently, a more complex picture of adult secondary HLH has emerged in which partial loss 363

of function–hypomorphic or dominant negative (including p.A433V identified in this cohort)–variants in 364

degranulation pathway members result in HLH-like manifestations with a sufficient immunologic 365

challenge26,28–33,37,47. Germline variants in immune-related genes have also been associated with patients 366

experiencing severe, hyperinflammatory manifestations of COVID-1963, including in STXBP230 and other 367

perforin degranulation pathway members64,65. Importantly, despite being referred to as ‘benign’ or ‘likely 368

benign’ in clinical variant databases such as ClinVar, STXBP2 putative deleterious variants from 4 of the 369

6 patients in our study have been recurrently identified in HLH patients37,39–41,43,44 and demonstrated to 370

functionally impair degranulation31,38,42. We hypothesize that the engineered nature of CAR-T cell 371

therapy, where high-affinity binders drive supraphysiologic T cell activation against many target cells, 372

represents an extreme immunologic challenge for T cells and the immune system overall. This “stress 373

test” may have the capacity to unmask or exacerbate hypomorphic protein functions that would otherwise 374

have minimal or undetectable clinical penetrance. 375

376

Importantly, most of the toxicity in our combined toxicity endpoint was driven by high-grade neurologic 377

toxicity rather than CRS, the former of which was more abundant in ZUMA-1 and ZUMA-7 overall. The 378

toxicity in these subjects is similar to real-world outcome studies of individuals receiving axicabtagene 379

ciloleucel outside the confines of a clinical trial66,67. Overall, axicabtagene ciloleucel and its companion 380

other hyperinflammatory contexts (e.g., Covid1930,71) without necessarily resulting in overt HLH. Finally, 385

current models of CAR-T cell neurotoxicity link central myeloid cell (microglia) activation as the key 386

driver of this pathology72,73. Degranulation defects in CAR-T cells could drive excessive myeloid 387

activation systemically and in the central nervous system as a putative mechanism. The contributions of 388

defects in HLH-associated genes in myeloid and other cell types remain unexplored in this study and may 389

be important contributors to the pathophysiology of CRS and neurologic toxicity. 390

391

While STXBP2 putative deleterious variants were enriched in the toxicity cohort in ZUMA-1, this was not 392

seen in ZUMA-7. Importantly, ZUMA-1 was a much more heavily pre-treated group of patients, with 393

69% having received ≥3 lines of therapy and 77% having undergone an autologous stem cell transplant, 394

versus ZUMA-7 patients, who were primary refractory or relapsed disease within 12 months and thus 395

received only a single line of therapy. ZUMA-1 subjects were also more likely to have high-stage disease 396

(85% vs 77% with stage III or IV disease). ZUMA-1 patients also had substantially higher levels of peak 397

and AUC CAR-T cells in the toxicity cohorts than ZUMA-7 and higher baseline levels of inflammation. 398

Given the rapidly evolving nature of toxicity management and grading, these findings do not invalidate 399

our findings with respect to STXBP2, and additional larger studies will be needed to explore this complex 400

association more fully, given the relative rarity of the discovery variants. 401

expansion, most notably with PTPN22 variant carriers who had the highest expansion in both of our 404

cohorts, despite making up just 5% of all subjects. While disruption of PTPN22 in T-cells and across the 405

One limitation of our findings is that the potential generalizability to other CAR-T cell designs, target 409

antigens, tumor types, or ancestral populations will need to be confirmed in future studies. Furthermore, 410

we used CRISPR-Cas9 to generate near-complete loss-of-function mutations or the overexpression of 411

variant proteins, which may not exactly recapitulate the behavior of the individual heterozygous variants 412

we identified in patients. 413

414

Unlike most traditional pharmacologic compounds in which there is a single, molecularly defined “active 415

ingredient,” autologous CAR-T cells are bespoke, living drugs that carry all the ancestral polymorphisms 416

of the individual from whom they are manufactured. This has important implications for CAR-T cell 417

behavior. Allogeneic CAR-T (allo-CAR-T) cells, in which a single healthy donor’s T cells may be used to 418

manufacture CAR-T cells for potentially several individuals, are currently being tested in numerous 419

clinical trials74. Our work suggests that germline-level donor screening may have implications for product 420

behavior since a single donor may provide T cells sufficient for dozens to hundreds of CAR-T cell 421

products. 422

423

In summary, our study establishes the first clear association between germline variants and CAR-T cell 424

behavior. We anticipate that this highly annotated dataset, incorporating whole genome sequencing 425

matched to two clinical trials of CAR-T-treated aggressive lymphoma patients, will provide further 426

valuable insights into the relationship between germline variants and engineered immune cell behavior. 427

METHODS 759

Study design and population of patients 760

We obtained available genomic DNA from patients in the ZUMA-1 and ZUMA-7 clinical trials. All 761

patients had provided written informed consent as part of the ZUMA-1 and ZUMA-7 studies at their 762

respective institutions. None of the authors of this manuscript had access to identifiable patient 763

information and nor did they participate in the consent process for the individuals. We stratified the 764

patients a priori into a case-control study design, with the toxicity (case) cohort defined as individuals 765

who had severe (Grade 3 or higher out of 5, with higher scores indicating more severe toxicity) cytokine 766

release syndrome (CRS; graded by Lee criteria75) or neurotoxicity (graded by CTCAE 4.03) or had 767

received the interleukin-6 (IL-6) cytokine receptor blocker tocilizumab with the presumption that the 768

latter represented a proxy for clinically significant CRS. The remainder (Grade 0-2 CRS or neurotoxicity 769

and did not receive tocilizumab) were designated the control cohort. No patients had previously 770

undergone allogeneic stem cell transplant. 771

772

Whole genome sequencing and Evaluation of Sequencing Read Coverage 773

Genomic DNA (gDNA) was extracted from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) of all de- 774

identified subjects, and we performed whole genome sequencing at the Broad Institute (Cambridge, MA) 775

to a mean sequencing depth of at least 30X on an Illumina HiSeqX (Illumina, San Diego, CA) with 150 776

base paired-end reads. Samples with sufficient total DNA quantity underwent PCR-free WGS (ZUMA-1: 777

n=84, ZUMA-7: n=134) while samples with relatively low DNA quantity underwent PCR amplification 778

before WGS (ZUMA-1: n=2, ZUMA-7: n=16). Raw sequencing Binary Alignment Map (BAM) files 779

were aligned to the human reference genome GRCh38  using BWA (version 0.7.15).76 The average 780

sample-level sequencing coverage for exome-wide intervals was calculated using GATK77 (version 3.7) 781

tool “DepthofCoverage” to ensure sufficient read depth to make confident germline calls. BAM files for 782

all samples included in the analysis had a sample mean coverage of over 25X across the genome. 783

project reference samples87 (n=2,504) with known continental ancestries of Admixed American (AMR), 795

African (AFR), European (EUR), East Asian (EAS), and South Asian (SAS). The combined file was 796

filtered for germline variants in the highly covered exome intervals (>15x). Then the filtered VCF file 797

was loaded into a “Hail” matrix table (version 0.2.11, https://github.com/hail-is/hail), and rare germline 798

variants of a cohort-level allele frequency below 1% and deviating from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium 799

(chi-squared p-value <1x10-6 ) were excluded. Then, we performed linkage disequilibrium (LD) pruning 800

using the “ld_prune” method in Hail to exclude variants with Spearman correlation coefficient >0.1 801

within a 1 million base pair window. These filtered germline variants were used for PCA with the Hail 802

“hwe_normalized_pca” method. Sklearn package (version 0.20.0) “RandomForestClassifier” function 803

was then applied to the top 10 global principal components of reference samples from 1000 Genomes 804

Project to train random forest classifiers for the five continental ancestries. This was used to assign broad 805

continental ancestry to the cases and controls. Given the limited number of non-EUR patients, only EUR 806
